items.name: The Substance
items.desc:
An unhinged nightmare about what happens when you take “I wish I was younger” a little too seriously.

A once-famous aerobics queen gets pushed out of the spotlight the second she’s deemed “too old,” because in her world a woman’s value basically has an expiry date. Desperate to stay relevant, she takes a sketchy glow-up drug that literally creates a younger, hotter version of herself to take her place.

At first it’s all perfect skin, perfect body, and everyone obsessed again, but sharing a life with your own younger replacement quickly turns into jealousy, identity crises, and some very melty, very not-glam side effects.

items.desc: romantic

items.name: Steins;Gate: The Movie − Load Region of Déjà Vu
items.desc: Steins;Gate: The Movie – Load Region of Déjà Vu is a love letter to the series that trades high-concept chaos for something more intimate and quietly devastating.  Set after the events of the anime, the film explores what happens when the cost of saving the world doesn’t end with a final choice. Memories blur, reality wavers, and the emotional toll of defying fate comes due. Rather than escalating the stakes with bigger conspiracies, the movie zooms in on identity, loss, and the terrifying idea of being forgotten—not just by history, but by the people who matter most.  It’s slower, more reflective, and deeply character-driven, giving the cast room to breathe and feel the weight of everything they’ve been through. The sci-fi mechanics are still clever and satisfying, but they exist in service of a powerful emotional core that hits hardest if you’re already attached to these characters.  If Steins;Gate is about fighting destiny, the movie is about living with the scars afterward—and why some connections are strong enough to pull someone back from the edge of existence itself. 🕰️💔

items.name: A taste of honey
items.desc: A Taste of Honey (1961) is a landmark British New Wave film directed by Tony Richardson, adapted from Shelagh Delaney's play, starring Rita Tushingham as a working-class teenager in industrial Manchester who becomes pregnant by a Black sailor and finds an unlikely ally in a gay art student. Known for its "kitchen sink realism," it tackles themes of class, race, and sexuality with a sensitive, modern approach, earning critical acclaim and awards, including BAFTAs for Tushingham and Dora Bryan (who plays her mother).
